strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant practical problem: combining parameter-efficient adaptation with deployable low-bit weights. Quantizing the merged base weights and LoRA update provides a coherent way to remove the separate high-precision adapter path without QA-LoRA’s structural restrictions.

The evaluation covers multiple model families and sizes, two quantization precisions, seven commonsense tasks, and zero/few-shot MMLU. The reported accuracy improvements are encouraging, particularly at 3 bits: LLaMA-2 7B reaches 61.3% commonsense accuracy versus 57.4% for QAT-LoRA.

The paper measures practical costs alongside accuracy. Reported 7B training memory is 25.4 GB, close to LoRA’s 25.1 GB and substantially below full QAT’s 79.5 GB. Using the same quantized inference kernel for merged and unmerged models provides a useful control for adapter overhead.
The forward-path diagrams communicate the method clearly. Detailed task results and ablations of initialization, adapter rank, and quantization group size help readers examine the reported behavior.
weaknesses: Baseline fidelity remains unresolved. Uniform-quantization versions of QLoRA and LoftQ provide useful controlled comparisons, but do not establish superiority over their original configurations. More seriously, Section 4.1 states that adapters use Kaiming initialization for A and zero initialization for B, without explaining an exception for LoftQ’s essential SVD initialization. LoftQ’s near-chance 3-bit MMLU results warrant verification before supporting broad comparative claims.

The efficiency comparisons are partly confounded. Appendix D uses a training context of 128 tokens only for L4Q on the 33B model, versus 2048 for the other settings. Consequently, its 33B memory and training-time comparisons do not isolate the method’s contribution. Total training times also use different training lengths; comparable context lengths, explicit token accounting, and validation-based time-to-quality comparisons are needed.

The explanation of memory savings needs a stronger control. With frozen base weights, full parameter gradients need not persist across layers; QAT-LoRA can also use transient dense intermediates to compute quantizer gradients. The paper does not separate savings from its custom backward implementation from savings specific to quantizing merged weights. A similarly optimized QAT-LoRA baseline and a breakdown of saved tensors would substantiate this central claim.

The backward specification is ambiguous at an important point. For dense weight gradient G and elementwise clipping mask M, the adapter gradients should be dA = alpha B^T(M ⊙ G) and dB = alpha(M ⊙ G)A^T. Equations 29–30 instead place a weight-shaped condition around adapter-shaped gradients without specifying this contraction order. This may be shorthand, but the custom implementation needs precise equations or reference code. Reproduction is further hindered by missing LoRA scaling and microbatch/gradient-accumulation settings, and unclear distinctions between iterations and optimizer steps.

Several improvements over the strongest baselines are only 0.1–0.3 percentage points, with no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals. Superiority is also not universal: in Table 3, LLaMA-2 13B obtains 50.0% five-shot MMLU versus QLoRA’s 50.6%. The core construction and experimental breadth make Findings plausible, but the unresolved baseline, efficiency-control, and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
